newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Big field baffles voters in local Russian poll.
newsitem.headline: Big field baffles voters in local Russian poll.

text.p: The people of Tula, baffled by an extravagent field of candidates led by President Boris Yeltsin's confidant turned enemy, General Alexander Korzhakov, voted for a new member of parliament on Sunday.

The by-election contest, which has brought a media circus to the impoverished industrial city, also includes chess champion Anatoly Karpov, a local businessman awaiting trial for extortion and a local democrat who calls the poll a farce.
But the wife of the founder of Russia's most notorious pyramid scheme was thrown off the ballot paper by a local court on Saturday for using improper campaigning methods.
The court said Yelena Mavrodi, a 27-year-old former model whose husband was behind the failed MMM pyramid scheme, had violated fund-raising rules.
Two-star general Korzhakov, sacked by Yeltsin as his personal bodyguard last year in a purge of Kremlin hawks, is the favourite in local opinion polls to win the vacant seat in the State Duma.

He startled the sleepy city of some 500,000 voters with an aggressive Yeltsin-style campaign, bringing rock stars and comedians to campaign for him, holding public meetings and overwhelming the local media with his advertising.
But his lead in the opinion polls was not confirmed by a random Reuters exit poll early on Sunday.

Voters at the bleak House of Metallurgy Workers, most of them elderly and middle-aged, said they needed a candidate who would defend local interests, get more money from the central budget and help revive Tula's ailing economy.
"We need somebody in the State Duma (lower house) who can make our lives better," said Vera, a worker in her 50s.
But voters appeared divided over who is best placed to help them -- a local politician or a Moscow-based outsider.
"I am for Korzhakov," said Yelena, an engineer. "He is a fighter, he has sharp teeth and he knows how to pull strings in Moscow."
But only one man recalled that Korzhakov's campaign had been launched by popular general Alexander Lebed, who held the Tula Duma seat until he became Yeltsin's security chief last summer.
Lebed, sacked in October, is now Yeltsin's most prominent opponent. He first backed Korzhakov, but then distanced himself from the burly 47-year-old, calling him "a mere bodyguard".
Korzhakov, a close Yeltsin friend for 10 years, has presented himself as a victim of a Kremlin plot and pledged to make public "compromising materials" against the establishment.
But the general still faces a strong challenge from Karpov and five local candidates.
Karpov, born in Tula, says his experience in the old Soviet parliament allowed him to learn enough to help Tula.
"I voted for Karpov," said pensioner Yekaterina. "He is from Tula, calm and has good foresight as a chess player."
Local democratic leader Eduard Pashchenko, a fiery orator, says Moscow-based candidates pursue their own political interests and he dismisses their campaign as a farce.
Businessman Nikolai Novikov, awaiting trial in prison on charges of extortion, views the charges as a plot by the local authorities to blacken his name.
The election will be decided on a first-past-the-post basis, provided that at least 25 percent of voters turn out.
Preliminary results are expected on Monday.
